title: Chain of Responsibility: request validation pipeline, approval workflow.
shortTitle: Design using the Chain of Responsibility pattern
topicTitle: Behavioral: Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template
keyPoints: The Chain of Responsibility passes a request through a line of handlers until one handles it or the chain ends.
Each handler holds a reference to the next handler and either processes the request or forwards it.
The pattern suits two jobs: a validation pipeline where all checks must pass, and an approval workflow where the first capable handler acts.
Adding a new validation or approval level is a new handler class inserted into the chain, satisfying Open/Closed.
A request that no handler accepts must have a clear default outcome, not silently vanish.
The chain can be built dynamically from configuration, making it flexible for different branches or times of day.

s1_definition.oneliner: The Chain of Responsibility passes a request through a line of handlers until one handles it or all have run.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Chain of Responsibility** – passes a request along a chain of handlers, each deciding to process it or forward to the next.
- **Handler** – holds a reference to the next handler and a `handle()` method.
- **Validation pipeline** – every handler checks one rule; all must pass for the request to proceed.
- **Approval workflow** – each handler checks its authority; the first capable handler processes and stops.
- **Extensibility** – adding a new step is inserting a new handler with zero changes to existing ones.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the Chain as a loan approval route at National Bank of India. Rajesh's loan request passes first to the clerk, then the branch manager, then the regional head, each approving within their limit or escalating. The request flows down the chain until someone handles it or it runs out of handlers.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Validation Pipeline
  ───────────────────
  Request ──→ AmountValidator ──→ KycValidator ──→ LimitValidator
              (positive?)         (KYC done?)      (within limit?)
              All must pass for the request to proceed.
```

```text
  Approval Workflow
  ─────────────────
  Request (INR 3,00,000)
       │
       ▼
  Clerk (limit: 50K)  ──→ cannot handle
       │
       ▼
  Officer (limit: 5L) ──→ APPROVED
       │
  (Manager never reached)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a line of handlers, each deciding whether to process it or forward it to the next. This decouples the sender from the receivers and turns a monolithic validator or a giant if-else into a set of small, independent handlers that can be reordered, enabled, disabled, or extended freely.

The pattern suits two classic jobs. A validation pipeline runs every handler in sequence: each checks one rule, and all must pass. An approval workflow has each handler check its authority, and the first capable handler processes and stops. Adding a new step is a new handler class inserted into the chain with zero changes to existing handlers, which is the Open/Closed principle.

The big design advantage is that each handler is trivially testable in isolation because it does one thing, and the chain can be built dynamically from configuration so different branches or times of day get different rules. The critical safety rule is that a request that no handler accepts must have an explicit default outcome rather than silently vanishing.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj builds transfer validation and loan approval using Chain of Responsibility. A regulated money operation must pass a precise, auditable sequence of independent checks, and the chain lets the team compose and evolve that sequence safely.

Remember one sentence: Chain of Responsibility passes a request through independent handlers, decoupling the sender from the receivers and making the processing pipeline freely extensible.
